title: India Marks Eye Donation Fortnight With Two Million Still Facing Corneal Blindness
excerpt: LVPEI's eye bank network has collected over 170,000 corneas since 1989, but India still performs only a fraction of the transplants it needs each year.
body:
• Over two million Indians live with corneal blindness, and 60 percent of those affected are children under 12.
  • India needs roughly 100,000 corneal transplants each year but can deliver only 25,000 to 30,000.
  • The L V Prasad Eye Institute's eye bank network has collected over 170,000 donor corneas since 1989, making it India's largest provider of sight-restoring tissue.
  • Misconceptions about disfigurement, age limits and medical eligibility continue to discourage potential donors, widening the gap between supply and demand.

India's 41st National Eye Donation Fortnight, running from August 25 through September 8, has drawn fresh attention to a stubborn public health crisis: the country is home to roughly 1.1 million people living with corneal blindness, yet its healthcare system manages only a fraction of the transplants needed to restore their sight.

According to data highlighted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare during the fortnight's launch, India requires about 100,000 corneal transplants annually. It performs between 25,000 and 30,000 — leaving a gap that continues to widen as awareness and donation rates lag far behind demand.

A Crisis That Hits Children Hardest

The numbers carry an uncomfortable skew toward the young. Over two million Indians are affected by corneal blindness, and 60 percent of them are below the age of 12, according to the L V Prasad Eye Institute (LVPEI). Corneas turn opaque due to infections, injuries, nutritional deficiencies such as Vitamin A shortage, or birth-related diseases. The only known cure is transplantation using tissue from a deceased donor.

Dr. Aravind Roy, a cornea and anterior segment specialist at LVPEI's Vijayawada campus, pointed to a recent study finding that India has the highest prevalence of moderate to severe visual impairment and blindness due to corneal diseases among all Asian countries. "Improving awareness on eye donation and enhancing capacity building in eye banking is the way forward to address corneal blindness in the country," he said.

LVPEI's Eye Bank Network: 170,000 Corneas and Counting

Established in 1987, LVPEI operates one of the most extensive eye-banking networks in the world. Its five facilities — in Hyderabad, Bhubaneswar, Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Kadapa — have collectively harvested over 170,626 donor corneas since 1989. The Ramayamma International Eye Bank in Hyderabad alone has collected more than 123,800 corneas and distributed over 71,000 for transplantation.

The institute's Shantilal Shanghvi Cornea Institute crossed a historic milestone in August 2024, completing its 50,000th corneal transplant — a feat no other single institution globally has matched over a comparable timeframe. LVPEI is also a World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for the Prevention of Blindness and provides more than half its services at no cost to patients.

"Eye donation can happen only after the death of a person and consent from family members is mandatory. Therefore, it is equally important for persons pledging their eyes to inform their family members and request them to honour their wishes after their passing."

— Dr. Sunita Chaurasia, Medical Director, Ramayamma International Eye Bank

Myths That Hold Donation Back

Despite decades of awareness campaigns, misconceptions continue to suppress donation rates. Some potential donors fear the retrieval process will disfigure the face. Others believe only younger people are eligible, or assume that conditions like diabetes, hypertension or prior cataract surgery disqualify them.

Dr. Sushmitha Sriganesh, Executive Director of Shraddha Eye Bank, told The Indian Practitioner that most of these beliefs are unfounded. Eye banks carefully assess donated tissue for suitability, and the process is designed to preserve the donor's dignity. Making a pledge, she noted, is only the first step — families need to be informed so they can provide consent and facilitate the donation when the time comes.

Scaling Up: 60,000 Transplants by 2030

Dr. Gullapalli Nageswara Rao, LVPEI's founder, has outlined an ambitious roadmap to double India's transplant capacity from 30,000 to 60,000 annually by 2030. The plan calls for establishing at least 50 standard eye banks nationwide — each requiring an investment of around Rs 1 crore — along with hospital cornea retrieval programs in 500 major hospitals staffed by trained grief counselors, and the training of 500 additional ophthalmic surgeons.

How the Diaspora Can Help

For Indians abroad, the corneal blindness crisis may feel geographically distant, but there are concrete ways to contribute. NRIs can pledge their eyes through Indian consulates and embassy programs, support LVPEI and other eye banks financially, and help fund the expansion of retrieval infrastructure in smaller cities. Perhaps most simply, they can have conversations with family members in India about the importance of donation and consent. The 41st Eye Donation Fortnight is a reminder that restoring someone's sight often begins with a single conversation at home.
